The remaining papers concern fracture-fixation biomechanics and implant design. These are **core-award links**, not outputs attributable solely to the FY2021 application.

calls.output: {'type': 'text', 'text': '{"project":{"appl_id":10150838,"fy":2021,"full_project_num":"5R01EB029207-02","core_project_num":"R01EB029207","subproject_id":null,"title":"Fracture Fixation Biomechanics Simulator with Adaptive Virtual Coaching","abstract":"Project Summary Obtaining proper biomechanical stability to promote healing is a primary goal of fracture fixation surgical procedures. Subpar fracture fixation can result in fracture nonunion, residual deformity, implant failure, disuse atrophy, osteopenia, and short or long-term disability. Patients present with variable fracture geometries, bone quality, activity level. Surgeons have many choices for implant types, sizes, materials, construct configurations, and postoperative weightbearing strategies. All these factors, as well as the patient?s innate fracture healing capacity, affect postoperative biomechanics and resulting clinical outcome. Community orthopaedic surgeons who are not trauma specialists often need to treat these fractures. Although surgical technique has received much attention in the medical simulation literature, there is increased recognition of the importance of simulation in the cognitive and decision-making aspects of surgery. The proposed project develops and tests a new interactive simulation software that enables a surgeon to make changes to patient variables and fracture fixation plan, and immediately visualize how these changes affect clinically important 3D biomechanics. The technology is enabled by our high-throughput simulation approaches for generation of precomputed results libraries. The project relies on close long-term collaborations between academic biomedical engineers and clinician scientists, enhanced by collaboration with a leading open-source visualization software research and development organization. The project tests the hypothesis that interactive visualization of 3D biomechanics in fracture fixation will improve biomechanical knowledge and fracture fixation plans. Specific Aim 1 develops and tests effectiveness of a refined simulation software, combined with an instructor-led session, for education of 3D fracture fixation biomechanics. The rich interface will include validated parametric simulations of three fundamental fracture fixation types (bridge plating, compression plating, and intramedullary nailing) applied to both simplified bones and to proximal femur fractures. Specific Aim 2 introduces an autonomous, adaptive virtual coach integrated into the software. The virtual coach will enable flexible, personalized training for each surgeon based on their progress. The project will provide new, exciting opportunities for providing deeper biomechanical understanding to the surgeons who create fracture fixation constructs, facilitating precision medicine and promoting safer and more effective surgical procedures.","phr":"Project Narrative Surgical care of fractures is an important part of modern orthopaedics, but subpar surgical decisions can result in fracture nonunion, residual deformity, implant failure, or long term disability. According to `outputs_get_project_detail`:

- **Title:** Advanced Computing/Computational Core
- **Institution / lead:** Stanford University; Stephen A. Baccus
- **FY / award:** FY2021; **5P30EY026877-05**, subproject **7083**

- **Administering institute:** National Eye Institute

The core supports vision research through shared **data storage, high-performance computing, high-speed networking, system administration and programming services**. It also helps laboratories adapt and exchange specialized software and algorithms for computational modeling and analysis. Its biomedical purpose is to enable analysis of large human and animal datasets to understand vision and eye disease.

## Application 10213736

According to `outputs_get_project_detail`:

- **Title:** Advanced Computing/Computational Core
- **Institution / investigator:** Stanford University; Stephen A. Baccus
- **Funding:** National Eye Institute, P30 research-center mechanism
- **Record:** FY2021, award **5P30EY026877-05**, subproject **7083**
- **Core project:** **P30EY026877**
- **Recorded project period:** September 30, 2017–June 30, 2022

The core supports vision research through **data storage, high-performance computing, system administration, and programming services**. It maintains Stanford’s Virtual Computing Service and helps laboratories adapt and share specialized software and algorithms for computational modeling and analysis. Its stated purpose is to enable storage and analysis of large human and animal datasets needed to understand vision and eye disease.

## Publications linked to P30EY026877

`outputs_get_project_publications` reports **678 linked publication records**, returning only the **100 newest**, spanning **2024–2025**. Of those returned, **64 have MeSH indexing** and **100 have iCite records**, although some citation-impact fields are missing.

The returned publications cover several broad themes:

| Theme | Representative publication |
|---|---|
| **AI and clinical prediction** | *Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Models Predicting Glaucoma Progression Using Electronic Health Records and Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer Scans* (2025), [PMID 40152766](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40152766/) |
| **Computational methods** | *Accelerated Simulation of Multi-Electrode Arrays Using Sparse and Low-Rank Matrix Techniques* (2025), [PMID 40031840](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40031840/) |
| **Distributed model training** | *Distributed training of foundation models for ophthalmic diagnosis* (2025), [PMID 39843622](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39843622/) |
| **Virtual-reality vision testing** | *Glaucoma Home Self-Testing Using VR Visual Fields and Rebound Tonometry…: A Pilot Study* (2024), [PMID 39102241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39102241/) |
| **Retinal prostheses and imaging** | *Enhancing prosthetic vision by upgrade of a subretinal photovoltaic implant in situ* (2025), [PMID 40118873](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40118873/) |
| **Neuroprotection and regeneration** | *Optineurin-facilitated axonal mitochondria delivery promotes neuroprotection and axon regeneration* (2025), [PMID 39979261](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39979261/) |

Other returned work addresses corneal biomaterials, retinal genetics, cataract surgery, pediatric vision, and population-level ophthalmic outcomes.

**Important limitation:** These links are at the **whole-award level**, not specifically attributable to this computational subproject or its FY2021 activity. The list also includes reviews, editorials, letters, and preprints—including some preprint/journal versions of the same work—so **678 linked records should not be interpreted as 678 distinct original studies**.

This is a descriptive summary for expert review, not a new NITRD classification.

- **Institution / PI:** Stanford University; Stephen A. Baccus

- **Administering institute:** National Eye Institute

The core provides shared **data storage, high-performance computing, system administration, and programming support** for vision research. It supports Stanford’s Virtual Computing Service and helps laboratories exchange and adapt specialized software and algorithms for computational modeling and analysis. Its stated purpose is to enable storage and analysis of large human and animal datasets needed to understand vision and eye disease.

The public record includes an existing **NITRD spending-category tag**, alongside Data Science, Bioengineering, vision disorders, and Neurosciences. This is a reported tag, not a new classification assessment.

## Application 10213736

**“Advanced Computing/Computational Core”** is a Stanford University vision-research core led by **Stephen A. Baccus**, administered by the **National Eye Institute**.

- **Record:** FY2021; award **5P30EY026877-05**, subproject **7083**.
- **Core project:** **P30EY026877**.
- **Purpose:** Provide shared data storage, high-performance computing, system administration and programming support for vision research. It also helps laboratories exchange and adapt specialized software and algorithms for computational modeling and analysis.
- **Scientific relevance:** Support acquisition, storage and analysis of large human and animal datasets used to understand vision and eye disease.
- **Recorded project period:** September 30, 2017–June 30, 2022. Total cost is unavailable.

*Source: `outputs_get_project_detail`.*

## Publications linked to P30EY026877

`outputs_get_project_publications` reports **678 linked publication records**, returning only the **100 newest**, dated **2024–2025**. These links are **at the core-award level**, not specifically attributable to this computational subproject or its FY2021 work.

The returned publications span:
- **AI and computational methods:** ophthalmic diagnosis, glaucoma prediction, surgical-performance assessment, foundation models and electrode-array simulation.
- **Imaging and vision technology:** adaptive optics, optical coherence tomography, virtual-reality testing and retinal prostheses.
- **Retinal biology and treatment:** neuroprotection, optic-nerve regeneration, genetics, corneal repair and drug delivery.
- **Clinical and population research:** surgical outcomes, eye-disease epidemiology, health disparities and ophthalmology education.

Thus, **678 linked records should not be interpreted as 678 distinct research studies**. Topic summaries above reflect titles and indexing, not full-text review.

## Application 10213736

According to `outputs_get_project_detail`:

- **Title:** Advanced Computing/Computational Core
- **Institution / PI:** Stanford University / Stephen A. Baccus
- **Record:** FY2021, award **5P30EY026877-05**, subproject **7083**
- **Core project:** **P30EY026877**
- **Administering institute:** National Eye Institute
- **Project dates:** September 30, 2017–June 30, 2022

The core provides shared **data storage, high-performance computing, system administration, and programming support** for vision research. It supports Stanford’s Virtual Computing Service and helps laboratories exchange and adapt specialized software and algorithms for computational modeling and analysis. Its biomedical purpose is to enable analysis of large human and animal datasets to understand vision and eye disease.

The public record includes NITRD and Data Science spending tags. No new classification was performed.

## Publications linked to P30EY026877

`outputs_get_project_publications` reports **678 linked publication records**, returning only the **100 newest**, dated **2024–2025**. These links are at the **whole-award level**, so they cannot all be attributed specifically to this computational subproject or its FY2021 work.

The returned publications cover several broad themes:

| Theme | Representative publication |
|---|---|
| **AI and clinical prediction** | “Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Models Predicting Glaucoma Progression Using Electronic Health Records and Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer Scans” — *Translational Vision Science & Technology*, 2025; [PMID 40152766](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40152766/) |
| **Distributed machine learning** | “Distributed training of foundation models for ophthalmic diagnosis” — *Communications Engineering*, 2025; [PMID 39843622](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39843622/) |
| **Computational methods** | “Accelerated Simulation of Multi-Electrode Arrays Using Sparse and Low-Rank Matrix Techniques” — *IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering*, 2025; [PMID 40031840](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40031840/) |
| **Retinal prostheses** | “Enhancing prosthetic vision by upgrade of a subretinal photovoltaic implant in situ” — *Nature Communications*, 2025; [PMID 40118873](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40118873/) |
| **VR-based vision testing** | “Glaucoma Home Self-Testing Using VR Visual Fields and Rebound Tonometry Versus In-Clinic Perimetry and Goldmann Applanation Tonometry: A Pilot Study” — *Translational Vision Science & Technology*, 2024; [PMID 39102241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39102241/) |
| **Retinal biology and neuroprotection** | “Optineurin-facilitated axonal mitochondria delivery promotes neuroprotection and axon regeneration” — *Nature Communications*, 2025; [PMID 39979261](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39979261/) |

Other topics include advanced retinal imaging, corneal biomaterials and repair, genetics and single-cell atlases, cataract surgery, and population-level ophthalmic outcomes.

**Limitations:** This is a summary of publication titles and metadata, not a full-text assessment of findings. The returned list includes reviews, editorials, and preprints; some studies appear as both preprint and journal records. All data come from a fixed snapshot loaded in October 2026, not a live search. This summary supports subject-matter review, not an official NITRD classification.
